Ann Arbor by the numbers

Which city office issues an Ann Arbor tax bill?

Ann Arbor collects its own property tax through the Treasury unit, and the city's Assessor sets the values behind each bill. Once real property tax stays unpaid past winter, the account moves to Washtenaw County.

The city's Assessing page reports that over half of Ann Arbor's revenue comes from property tax, so assessments draw close scrutiny. A bill is a combined figure: the city levy, plus the county, the schools and other taxing units, each setting its own millage.

A separate administration fee also appears. State law lets the city add up to 1 percent of the tax, and the money offsets the work of defending assessments and collecting for every taxing unit.

What dates matter on the Ann Arbor tax calendar?

Two bills arrive each year: summer tax is billed July 1 and winter tax December 1, with the last penalty-free days at the end of those months. County operating tax rides on the summer bill, and the voted county millages ride on the winter one.

Missing the winter deadline starts a short countdown. Real property tax still unpaid on February 28 is passed to the Washtenaw County Treasurer, and extra penalties and interest begin March 1. The city's online record stops at that handoff, so confirm with the county whether a late balance has been paid.

Key dates and payment points listed by the City of Ann Arbor Treasury
ItemDetail
Summer taxPayable from July 1, due July 31
Winter taxPayable from December 1, due December 31
Real property turned over to the countyAfter February 28 following the tax year
Summer deferment filing deadlineSeptember 15
Pay in personLarcom City Hall, 301 E. Huron St., weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Pay by mailCity of Ann Arbor Treasurer, P.O. Box 77602, Detroit, MI 48277-0602
Local bank branchesJuly and December only, with the original stub

How are Ann Arbor property taxes calculated?

Take the taxable value, divide by 1,000, multiply by the millage rate, then multiply by 1.01 for the fee. Taxable value often trails assessed value because Proposal A, passed by Michigan voters in 1994, ties its yearly growth to the smaller of 5 percent or inflation, with additions counted separately. Assessed value itself targets half of market value.

The city's estimator page shows annual millage totals of 52.8802 for principal residences and 68.8196 for other property. Run purely as arithmetic, a $200,000 taxable value at the first total comes to $10,681.80 with the fee included. Rates move from year to year, and your parcel's real bill follows the units that cover it.

Your taxable value is printed on the annual bill and on the assessment notice, which the city mails around the first week of March. The online property record card holds the figures behind both.

Why does an Ann Arbor tax bill jump after a sale?

Following a sale or transfer, the next tax year's taxable value is set equal to the assessed value, the half-of-market figure. Ann Arbor calls that uncapping. The yearly limit then applies again until ownership changes once more.

That rule is why a buyer's first full bill can top the one you paid. A long-held house may carry a taxable value well under its assessed value, and the buyer begins without that cushion. With homes valued at a median of $453,400, the difference can be sizable.

The Assessor's Office, on the fifth floor of Larcom City Hall, takes the Property Transfer Affidavit, the Principal Residence Exemption affidavit and the request to rescind that exemption. Hand them in, submit them on the online forms page or mail them. Ask questions at 734.794.6530 or assessor@a2gov.org.

How does a homeowner challenge an Ann Arbor assessment?

Start with the city Board of Review, which sits four days beginning the Monday of March's third week. You appear by appointment, and the Assessor hands out the appeal forms. Board members are appointed citizens, approved by council, and do not work for the city.

The case that works shows assessed value running past 50 percent of true cash value. Objecting that taxes keep climbing does not count, the city explains, because taxable value may rise yearly by inflation or 5 percent, whichever is lower. Helpful evidence includes comparable nearby sales, mistakes on your record card and a repair estimate for something like a leaking basement.

  • A homeowner has to protest at the local board before taking a case to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.
  • The Tribunal filing date is July 31 for homes, and May 31 for commercial and industrial real property and business personal property.
  • The board mails its decision some weeks after it adjourns, along with the next appeal steps.

Is a deferment available, and who handles a balance that went delinquent?

Certain owners can put off the summer bill: senior citizens, people with qualifying disabilities or blindness, and eligible servicepersons, veterans and their surviving spouses. A summer deferment carries a $40,000 household income cap. Pick up the application at the Customer Service Center, 301 E. Huron St., or find it at washtenaw.org, and file it with the treasurer by September 15.

Real property balances that moved to the county are handled by the Washtenaw County Treasurer at 734.222.6600 or taxes@washtenaw.org. Overdue personal property tax stays with the city, and 734.994.2833 gives the amount.

If you plan to sell with a bill outstanding, request the figures before you list. The closing agent pays what is owed from your proceeds.

What does an Ann Arbor seller need to know about the city?

Two land speculators founded Ann Arbor in 1824 and named it for their wives, both called Ann, and the bur oaks on the site. The town became the Washtenaw County seat in 1827, a village in 1833 and a city in 1851. The University of Michigan took root there in 1837, and the two grew up together.

The Huron River winds through town, and the Tree Town nickname rests on more than 50,000 street trees. Three freeways ring the city: I-94 on the south and west, US 23 on the east and M-14 on the north. Ann Arbor Public Schools runs the public high schools, among them Pioneer, Huron, Skyline and Community. The university alone employs about 30,000 workers, roughly 12,000 of them at the medical center.

  • Estimated 2025 population: 122,233, down 1.3 percent from the 2020 base.
  • Owners hold 45.5 percent of 50,499 households, which makes renters the majority.
  • Typical home value $453,400, typical gross rent $1,649.
  • Household income at the midpoint: $82,212; adults with a four-year degree or more: 77.9 percent.
  • Monthly owner costs at the midpoint: $2,436 with a mortgage, $1,036 without.

Renters fill more than half of Ann Arbor's homes, so some sellers are landlords or heirs with an older house. When repairs stand in the way of a conventional sale, a buyer who takes the property as-is can close without them.

More questions about Ann Arbor, MI Property Tax Guide

What is the due date for Ann Arbor summer tax?

July 31, with payments accepted from July 1. Winter tax runs on the same pattern, opening December 1 and closing December 31.

Where can I pay my Ann Arbor tax face to face?

Use the Customer Service and Payment Center inside Larcom City Hall, 301 E. Huron St., open weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. A drive-up drop box at East Ann Street and North Fifth Avenue stays open around the clock.

Does selling change an Ann Arbor taxable value?

Yes, for the buyer. The year after a transfer, taxable value is reset to the assessed value, a step the city calls uncapping.

When must an Ann Arbor homeowner file with the Michigan Tax Tribunal?

By July 31, after first protesting at the March Board of Review. Commercial and industrial real property and business personal property must file by May 31.

Who collects Ann Arbor real property tax that is still unpaid in March?

The Washtenaw County Treasurer, at 734.222.6600, takes real property tax not received by February 28. Delinquent personal property tax stays with the city.

Livonia by the numbers

Who bills and collects property tax in Livonia, Michigan?

The City of Livonia assesses and bills its own property tax, and Wayne County steps in only after a bill goes delinquent. The Assessment Department sets values and handles exemption forms. The Treasurer's Office, on the first floor of City Hall at 33000 Civic Center Drive, mails real and personal property tax bills on July 1 and December 1 and collects the payments.

Those payments are split among several taxing bodies listed by the city: the City of Livonia, Livonia Public Schools, Clarenceville Public Schools, Schoolcraft College, the State of Michigan education tax, Wayne County, Wayne County RESA and Oakland ISD. A house in the northeast corner of the city that falls in the Clarenceville district therefore carries a different mix of levies than one in the Livonia Public Schools territory.

  • Treasurer, bills, due dates, deferrals, special assessments, millage questions: (734) 466-2245.
  • Assessment Department, valuation and exemption forms: (734) 466-2220.
  • Water account: (734) 466-2278.
  • Inspection, for outstanding permits, violations, vacant or abandoned property registration fees and certificate of occupancy: (734) 466-2580.

When are Livonia property taxes due?

Summer taxes are billed July 1 and due September 14. Winter taxes are billed December 1 and due February 14. When a due date falls on a weekend or holiday, the due date moves to the next business day. Checks go to City of Livonia, Treasurer, 33000 Civic Center Drive, Livonia, MI 48154.

Livonia tax bill calendar and city fees
ItemRule
Summer billBilled July 1, due September 14
Winter billBilled December 1, due February 14
Returned payment$25 charge
Payment by a title, mortgage or servicing company without the original bill$5 duplicate bill fee
Unpaid real property tax after the city periodTurned over to the Wayne County Treasurer

The city says printouts or screenshots from its online system do not count as an original tax bill. A title company closing a Livonia sale should bring the original, or the $5 fee applies. Delinquent personal property tax stays with the city treasurer, while delinquent real property tax moves to the county.

How can I look up a Livonia tax bill and special assessments?

The city runs an online property inquiry system at livoniatax.org, using BS&A software. Agree to the disclaimer, search by address, and enter only the street name without Road, Street or Avenue, or just the house number. Click the property, open the Tax Information tab, and the taxes appear by year and season, with a detailed breakdown behind each year.

The city warns that errors on the site do not cancel taxes or special assessments owed, that the official records at City Hall cover current-year collections only, and that payments on delinquent taxes do not show online. To check a delinquent balance, contact the Wayne County Treasurer.

Special assessments are a separate item. Email specials@livonia.gov to request the status on a parcel. Vacant and abandoned property fees, permit issues and violations do not appear in the online system, so a seller who wants a clean closing should ask Inspection for those directly.

What exemptions and deferrals apply to a Livonia home?

The Assessment Department reminds homeowners of the principal residence exemption deadlines. An affidavit filed on or before June 1 earns the exemption on that year's summer and winter levy and later years while the home remains the owner's principal residence. One filed after June 1 and on or before November 1 applies to the current winter levy and later levies.

The city also publishes a form letting a homeowner defer the due date of winter taxes on a principal residence without penalty or interest, for a stated period set each year. Ask the Treasurer's Office which year's form and deadline applies. Wayne County adds that the poverty exemption is reached through the local assessing unit, so Livonia owners facing hardship should start with the Assessment Department, not the county.

Religious, charitable and educational exemption forms, plus personal property forms, are on the Assessment Department page, which accepts forms by email, mail or the City Hall drop box on the east side of the building.

What happens if Livonia property taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid summer and winter bills are forwarded to the Wayne County Treasurer. Wayne County lays out the state timeline this way: on March 1 unpaid taxes become delinquent at the county, adding a 4 percent administration fee and 1 percent interest per month. A $15 collection fee follows on October 1. The next March 1 the parcel forfeits to the county treasurer, with a $175 fee and recording fees, and interest rises to 1.5 percent per month retroactive to the first delinquency.

Foreclosure follows. Michigan's three-year process ends with the circuit court entering a judgment, and unpaid taxes on March 31 of the third year mean the owner loses the property. Wayne County sends at least ten notices before that point.

Owners with a financial hardship can apply for a Wayne County payment plan. Standards cited are 125 percent of the federal poverty level, and the application needs photo ID, a copy of the deed, proof of occupancy and proof of income. After a foreclosure, the former owner can claim remaining auction proceeds by filing a notice of intent by July 1 of that year.

What does it mean to sell a house in Livonia with tax due?

Livonia is a Wayne County city of about 95,500 people at the 2020 census, set roughly 20 miles northwest of downtown Detroit. It covers about 35.7 square miles of land, was organized as Livonia Township in 1835 and became a city in 1950. More than 40,000 housing units were counted in 2020, and only 2.7 percent were vacant. Ford, Trinity Health, Livonia Public Schools and St. Mary Mercy Hospital rank among the largest employers. Newburgh and Nankin lakes lie in the south and southwest, Hines Drive links them, and the Rosedale Gardens Historic District and the Laurel Park Place mall at Six Mile and Newburgh roads are among the places buyers know. The median age at the 2020 census was 45.6, and many homes here have been owned for decades, so a long-held house often has a taxable value well below its market value, a gap that closes for the next owner after a sale.

Most Livonia homes sold with tax due close like any other: the title company gets a payoff, pays the city or county from the seller's proceeds, and records the deed. If the bill is delinquent, ask Wayne County for the payoff figure, since City Hall no longer holds the balance. Owners behind on taxes, with an inherited house or a place that needs work, can ask for a cash offer and have the payoff settled at the table.

More questions about Livonia, MI Property Tax Guide

When is the Livonia summer tax due?

September 14. The summer bill is mailed July 1, and if September 14 lands on a weekend or holiday the due date becomes the next business day.

Where do I pay Livonia winter taxes?

Mail a check payable to the City of Livonia to Treasurer, 33000 Civic Center Drive, Livonia, MI 48154, or use the Treasurer's Office on the first floor of City Hall. Winter bills are due February 14.

Who do I call about a delinquent Livonia tax bill?

The Wayne County Treasurer. Delinquent real property taxes are turned over to the county, and the city's own records show current-year collections only.

How do I get the principal residence exemption in Livonia?

File the affidavit with the Assessment Department. Filing by June 1 covers that year's summer and winter taxes, and filing after June 1 through November 1 covers the winter levy.

Which school districts tax Livonia homes?

Livonia Public Schools serves most of the city, and a portion of the northeast is in Clarenceville Public Schools. Both appear among the bodies that receive the city's collections.

Cash Home Buyers in Michigan

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Novi, MI Property Tax Guide sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who bills what in Novi

  • Novi Assessing Department handles assessment.

Local notes

Behind on Novi property tax?
We buy Novi houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.
Get My Cash Offer →

Novi by the numbers

Which Novi offices send and collect the property tax bill?

Novi's own Treasurer's Office mails and collects the bills, while the city Assessing Department supplies the values behind them. The treasurer works from 45175 Ten Mile Road, Novi, MI 48375, and answers tax questions at 248-347-0440. The Treasurer page also links the online property and tax search.

Novi sits in Oakland County, about 25 miles northwest of downtown Detroit, and covers roughly 30 square miles of land around Walled Lake. I-96, I-696, I-275 and M-5 all reach the city, and the population rose from about 9,700 in 1970 to 66,243 in 2020. Novi became a city in 1969, after starting life as a township in 1832.

The city is only the collecting agent for most of what appears on the statement. Its own operating taxes are billed in full on the summer statement, while the winter statement carries the county, school and authority levies. Novi has no say over the county and school rates.

When are Novi property taxes due?

Two payment seasons apply: late summer and winter. The city's 2026 notice said summer bills would be mailed the week of July 1 and that payments had to reach the treasurer on or before August 31 to avoid an automatic penalty. For anyone reading after that date, the winter window is the one to watch.

Novi billing calendar, from the city's 2026 summer notice and its winter statement
StepTimingWhat applies
Summer bill mailedWeek of July 1 (2026 notice)Call the treasurer if nothing arrives by July 15
Summer deadlineAugust 31 (2026 notice)Postmarks and post-dated checks are not accepted
Winter payment windowDecember 1 to February 14Payment must be physically received by the treasurer
After February 14Late period3% automatic penalty that the treasurer cannot waive
From March 1Past-due stagePayable to the Oakland County Treasurer, with added charges

A drop box sits behind the Civic Center, and the 2026 notice accepted drop box payments until midnight on the deadline day. Online payment by credit card or electronic check is available through cityofnovi.org. Be careful with the bank numbers you type, because a returned payment after the due date draws the penalty.

How does Novi set the taxable value of a house?

The bill rests on taxable value, a figure that normally sits below half of what the house would fetch. The assessor estimates market value as of Tax Day, December 31 of the year before, and the assessed value is about 50% of that. For 2026 the city used a 24-month sales study running from April 1, 2023 to March 31, 2025, covering roughly 2,000 sales.

Taxable value grows more slowly than assessed value. The 2026 inflation rate multiplier is 1.027, so a home that stays with its owner can rise no more than 2.7%, even if neighborhood prices climbed 10%. The city's formula is the prior taxable value, less losses, times the multiplier, plus additions.

  • Taxable value is the lesser of assessed value and capped value.
  • The tax equals taxable value divided by 1,000, times the millage rate.
  • A sale resets the taxable value to the assessed value the following year.
  • Special assessments, trash charges and penalties are added on top.

After you sell, the next owner's bill will probably run higher than yours did. Tell any buyer to look at the assessed value rather than your old bill.

What is the process to appeal a Novi assessment?

Appeals start with the March Board of Review, the sole yearly chance to contest a current value. Hearings begin on the second Monday of March, after the Notice of Assessment goes out in mid February. Petition forms come from the Assessing Department or the city's website, and you make an appointment to appear.

If the board's answer is not acceptable, the next level is the Michigan Tax Tribunal. A residential petition must go to the Tribunal at 611 W. Ottawa St., Lansing, MI 48933 by July 31, and only after you have appeared before the March board. Commercial and industrial appeals to the Tribunal are due May 31. The July and December boards cannot hear value disputes under MCL 211.53b.

Two relief options sit outside the appeal process. Michigan has no age-based property tax break, but Novi offers an annual poverty exemption based on income and assets, which needs Board of Review approval. Owners who qualify can also ask the Treasurer's Office about deferring summer taxes.

What is a Novi tax bill spent on?

On the city's sample winter statement, about 59% of a homestead bill went to education, 30% to the City of Novi and 11% to Oakland County. That split was based on the Novi and OCC district homestead rates, so a parcel in another district will differ. Several school systems reach into the city.

  • Novi Community Schools cover most of the city.
  • Northville Public Schools serve a large part of the south side.
  • Walled Lake Consolidated Schools take in a pocket with two elementary schools.
  • South Lyon Community Schools hold a small western strip.

The statement's other lines include the county parks and recreation levy, the zoo authority, the art institute, Oakland transit and the Huron Clinton Metropolitan Authority. Check the parcel number and school district code on your own bill before you compare it with a neighbor's.

What do federal housing counts show for Novi?

Census QuickFacts lists 67,319 people in Novi for July 2025 and 26,801 households across 2020 to 2024. Owners live in 66.3% of housing units. The typical owned home is valued at $421,900, rent at the middle is $1,747 a month, and household income at the middle is $110,723.

A condo near the I-96 corridor and a lakeside house will sit well apart from those citywide figures. About 29% of residents were born abroad. Health care, automotive suppliers and the retail cluster around Novi Road and I-96 anchor the local economy.

What follows when Novi tax goes unpaid?

After the winter period closes, the balance moves to Oakland County. MCL 211.78a returns taxes still owed on March 1 as delinquent, adding a 4% county fee and interest at 1% for each month. The county treasurer collects from there, and ongoing nonpayment leads into a three-year foreclosure process.

For 2024 and earlier balances, the county's notices name March 31, 2027 as the final day to pay and keep the property. The treasurer's office, at 248-858-0611, offers repayment schedules and referrals. Our Oakland County property tax guide lays out the foreclosure calendar step by step.

What should a Novi seller do about the principal residence exemption?

The exemption takes up to 18 mills of school operating tax off a home you own and occupy. To see it on the summer bill, you had to be both owner and resident by June 1. People who moved in between June 2 and November 1 can claim a winter exemption.

On a sale, send the Assessing Department the rescission form so the exemption ends on the correct date. A seller who has already bought another Michigan residence may keep it on the old house through a conditional rescission, as long as the old house is listed, vacant, unleased and free of business use. Submit that form with the new exemption by June 1 for both bills, or by November 1 for winter only.

How does a Novi sale handle the tax bill?

At closing, the title company splits the current year's tax between seller and buyer and settles any unpaid amount out of your proceeds. Get the present balance from the city treasurer. If any year has moved to Oakland County, buy an official delinquent tax statement through the county's Property Gateway, which sells them to owners and title companies.

A sale can close with tax owing, since the payoff is a line on the seller's settlement statement. The avoidable cost is the late charge: miss the winter deadline and a 3% penalty applies that staff cannot waive. Pay early, and keep both statements for the year of the sale.

More questions about Novi, MI Property Tax Guide

When is the winter tax deadline in Novi?

February 14. The winter statement allows payment from December 1 through February 14, and the money has to be physically in the treasurer's hands by that day. A 3% penalty starts after it, and no one at the counter can waive it.

Will a postmark count as on-time in Novi?

No. The city's notices say postmarks and post-dated checks are refused. Use the drop box behind the Civic Center, pay online, or mail the check early enough to arrive on time.

Do taxes rise after buying a Novi house?

Often. The year after a sale, taxable value resets to the assessed value, which may sit well above the earlier capped figure. Later increases are limited to the inflation multiplier or 5%, whichever is smaller.

Which Novi department answers questions about my value?

The Assessing Department handles values, exemptions, and name or address changes. Bills and payments go through the Treasurer's Office at 248-347-0440.

Can a Novi house with tax behind still be sold?

Yes. The title company pays the balance, with penalty and interest, from your proceeds at closing. Request a current statement first from the city, or from the Oakland County Treasurer for earlier years.

Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $176,500 here, which is 8% below the middle figure for the 50 mi places. About 39% of households rent, so 61% own; the mi median for these places is 66% owner-occupied. Homes here were typically built in 1969, so the median house is about 54 years old. These numbers describe Westland as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.
